title: Zero to One, One to Ten, Ten to a Hundred: Three Ways of Working with AI
author: Anthea Roberts

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core view that effective deployment depends on domain expertise, understanding AI’s limitations and redesigning workflows rather than merely procuring tools. It materially extends that view with a multiplicative framework linking human expertise, AI expertise and system capability, though this contribution is conceptual and example-based rather than empirically validated.
qs: Here's the formula I keep coming back to: **human expertise × AI expertise × AI capability**.
Those systems work because the people behind them have deep domain expertise and deep AI expertise and they rebuilt everything from scratch to be human × AI native.

kp.k: Three AI relationships distinguish enablement, acceleration and transformation
kp.d: Roberts proposes a conceptual framework for AI use, illustrated primarily through software engineering: zero to one enables previously inaccessible activities; one to ten amplifies existing capabilities; ten to a hundred transforms workflows and possibilities. She explicitly treats these as different relationships rather than stages on a single ladder. The document does not directly discuss legal services.
qs: I've started thinking in three buckets: zero to one, one to ten, and ten to a hundred. These aren't points on a single ladder. They're different relationships with AI.

kp.k: Enablement opens activities previously blocked by skill barriers
kp.d: Roberts describes AI enabling non-programmers to build basic apps and specialists to acquire working knowledge in another field. She attributes the 'zone of excitement' framing to David Kaye. She qualifies the apparent ceiling on such activity: basic outputs and working knowledge need not be the user's endpoint.
qs: This is what happens when AI lets you do something you couldn't do before.
Someone with no programming background uses vibe coding to build a basic app. An expert in one field uses AI to get up to speed in another.
AI-assisted exploration produces working knowledge, not deep expertise. Sometimes true. But zero-to-one vibe coding can also be a gateway drug.

kp.k: Acceleration can shift bottlenecks into editing and review
kp.d: For people with existing expertise, Roberts argues that AI can accelerate drafting, first versions and repetitive work, but may also introduce friction. Faster generation can require longer editing, overwhelm review capacity or create excessive choices. She poses AI's contribution to both mastery and productivity as an open question rather than presenting measured tenfold gains.
qs: The second bucket is where you already have real capability and you're using AI to go faster, do better, or work at greater scale.
You produce text faster but spend longer editing. Code generates quickly but reviews bottleneck. You generate more options but drown in choices.
Could AI help to accelerate people on that journey to both mastery and productivity? That is the 1-10x question.

kp.k: Transformation requires domain expertise, AI fluency and workflow redesign
kp.d: Roberts distinguishes transformation from simply performing existing work faster. She argues that it requires deep domain expertise, understanding of AI systems and willingness to rebuild workflows. She reports Simon Willison's term 'vibe engineering' to distinguish this architectural, demanding approach from accessible, improvisational vibe coding.
qs: You're not doing the same things faster. You're rethinking what's possible.
This demands a rare combination: deep expertise in your domain, real fluency in AI, and willingness to tear up your existing workflow and start over.
Vibe coding is improvisational and accessible. Vibe engineering is architectural and demanding.

kp.k: Structured agents and feedback loops underpin compounding workflows
kp.d: Roberts cites Microsoft's Amplifier and Every's Compound Engineering as examples of designed workflows with specialized sub-agents and reflection loops that feed lessons into documentation. She presents these practices as mechanisms for progressively improving outputs. She also reports that Claude Code creator Boris Cherny described twelve workflow steps, including running between five and fifteen agents throughout his day, and interprets his approach as engineering redesigned rather than merely accelerated.
qs: He then listed twelve steps, including running between five and fifteen Claude Code agents throughout his day, each handling different parts of his work.
Both involve structured processes, designed workflows, sub-agents with specific jobs, and reflection loops that feed lessons back into documentation.
He wasn't using AI to do his old job faster. He was doing a different job.

kp.k: Transformative gains concern scope and scale, not just speed
kp.d: Roberts argues that redesigned AI workflows can enable entry into additional domains, experiments and projects that otherwise would not have been resourced, and iterative improvements in output. She explicitly cautions that most 100x claims are exaggerated and that relatively few people achieve this form of transformation. Extending these gains beyond software engineering is an interest she expresses, not a demonstrated result.
qs: They're scope: branching into domains you couldn't have tackled alone. They're scale: running experiments and projects you'd never have resourced.
And they're compounding: systems that learn so that outputs get closer to what you want each time you turn the crank.
But most 100x claims are exaggerated. This bucket is real, but hard. Far fewer people operate here than the discourse suggests.
I am increasingly interested in what this 10-100x gain might look like in knowledge work more generally, outside of software engineering.

kp.k: Established practitioners face a squeeze from both directions
kp.d: Roberts characterizes established practitioners using AI mainly for acceleration as potentially experiencing existential dread: newcomers can produce superficially similar work, while transformative users demonstrate workflows requiring unfamiliar skills and abandonment of established practices. She acknowledges that newcomers' outputs may be lower quality or difficult to maintain and debug; her argument concerns their perceived threat, not demonstrated equivalence in capability. She contrasts this middle group's experience with excitement among enabled beginners and transformative users.
qs: The people in the middle often feel what Kaye might call existential dread.
From below, zero-to-one people produce outputs that look like your work.
It doesn't matter if the quality is lower, if they couldn't maintain it or debug it when things break. The output exists. It looks like yours.
From above, you hear about 100x transformations, reimagined workflows, impossible scales. But that requires AI expertise you haven't built and abandoning workflows you spent years refining.

kp.k: AI mastery complements rather than replaces domain expertise
kp.d: Roberts recommends developing substantive AI fluency and redesigning workflows rather than relying on prompting tricks. Her conceptual formula makes human expertise, AI expertise and AI capability multiplicative conditions for compounding gains. She argues that existing craft skills are becoming baseline requirements rather than differentiators, while retaining an essential role for domain expertise. She acknowledges that not everyone will want to undertake this shift.
qs: The path from one-to-ten to ten-to-hundred isn't about prompting tricks. It requires real AI fluency.
Not just using tools but understanding how they work, what they're good at, where they fail.
It means accepting that craft skills you built are becoming table stakes, not differentiators.
human expertise × AI expertise × AI capability
Multiplicative, not additive. If any term is zero, the product is zero.
Your domain expertise isn't obsolete. It's one of the multipliers. But on its own, it's not enough anymore.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Roberts argues that AI enables new capabilities, accelerates existing work with qualifications, and can transform expert workflows; these are distinct relationships with AI rather than a single progression.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain discussion of software engineering and knowledge work, not a specific claim about legal services. Roberts argues that AI lets novices build basic applications and helps experts explore unfamiliar fields. For existing practitioners, AI can speed drafting and repetitive work, but editing, code review and excessive options can offset gains. More transformative use combines domain expertise, AI fluency and redesigned workflows, including specialised agents and feedback into documentation, to expand scope and scale and produce compounding improvements. Roberts also claims that established practitioners can feel squeezed between novices producing superficially similar outputs and advanced users transforming their work. She presents the extension of transformative gains beyond software engineering as an area of interest rather than an established finding.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Roberts supports the framework with personal experience, illustrative engineering workflows and linked commentary, not measured productivity or labour-market results.
pts.d: Roberts identifies herself as an avid Claude Code user and says she recognises practices in Boris Cherny's account of running five to fifteen agents. She interprets his workflow as an example of engineering transformation. She also cites Microsoft's Amplifier project and Every's Compound Engineering approach as examples of structured processes, specialised sub-agents and documentation feedback loops. Simon Willison's distinction between vibe coding and vibe engineering and David Kaye's emotional framing inform her analysis. These are examples and conceptual references: the document supplies no controlled comparisons, benchmarks or quantified evidence establishing tenfold or hundredfold gains. The multiplicative formula is Roberts's conceptual account, not a reported empirical model.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims describe current practices, with no dated forecast; transformative gains are conditional on substantial expertise and workflow redesign.
pts.d: In this source labelled 2025, Roberts describes enablement, acceleration and some transformative engineering practices as already occurring. She gives no timetable for wider adoption or extension to other knowledge work. She qualifies acceleration because downstream work can become a bottleneck, and qualifies transformation as difficult and uncommon. The three numerical labels are not established measured returns. Roberts argues that moving from acceleration toward transformation requires understanding AI's capabilities and failures, retaining deep domain expertise and being willing to rebuild established workflows. Novice use can lead to further development, but she does not claim that all users will progress.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are novices, established domain experts and AI-fluent expert practitioners, especially in software engineering.
pts.d: Novices gain access to activities they previously could not perform, although outputs may remain basic and users may lack maintenance or debugging skills. Established experts gain some productivity but can experience review burdens and perceived competitive pressure from both novice outputs and transformed expert workflows. Practitioners who combine domain knowledge with AI expertise can undertake a wider range and scale of projects. Roberts argues that domain expertise remains valuable but is insufficient on its own for this transformed mode of working. She does not identify effects on particular legal roles, law-firm segments, legal-service buyers or access to justice, and does not quantify employment or income effects.
